extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political science/comparative constitutional government
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter comparing the structural design, strengths, weaknesses, and practical effects of the American separated system and the European (parliamentary/cabinet) system of government. Focuses on separation of powers, party systems, conflict resolution, and crisis management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disqualification of executive office-holders from legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: They forbade 'any person holding office under the United States' to be a member of either House.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: prevent ministers, named by and acting under the President, from being his instruments rather than faithful representatives of the people; intended to keep the legislature 'pure, independent, vigilant' and the servant of the people. (Footnote compares English Act of Settlement tradition.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular (indirect) election of the President to ensure independence
rubrics_metrics.description: The people, through certain electors appointed for the purpose, choose the President, giving him the better status of a popular, though indirect, mandate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design rationale: makes the President independent of Congress and encourages use of the veto that a mere nominee of Congress might hesitate to use; intended to balance independence of Congress with that of the President.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish an authoritative constitutional court
rubrics_metrics.description: Creation of a court entitled to place an authoritative interpretation upon the Constitution in which the supreme will of the people was expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function: provides a remedy for disputes between branches and a security for faithful observance of the Constitution which a system with an omnipotent legislature (e.g., Britain) lacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation can make branches independent but weak
rubrics_metrics.description: They divided the legislature from the executive so completely as to make each not only independent, but weak even in its own proper sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: the President is fettered in foreign policy and appointments by the Senate; he is forbidden to appeal at a crisis from Congress to the country; Congress divided into two co-equal houses whose disagreement paralyzes legislative action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cabinet/parliamentary responsibility makes executive directly answerable to legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: The British House of Commons can displace ministers by a resolution of want of confidence, and compel the sovereign to employ such servants as it approves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical effect: ministry acts as the executive leadership of the Commons, is sensitive to party and public opinion, and can dissolve Parliament to seek a fresh mandate; this produces closer coordination between executive and legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-party equilibrium required for stable cabinet government
rubrics_metrics.description: The system presupposes the existence of two great parties and no more; parties each strong enough to restrain the violence of the other, yet one of them steadily preponderant in any given House of Commons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a third or fourth party appears, stability is disturbed: dissolutions become more frequent, and even dissolutions may fail to restore stability. Example: difficulties in the Third French Republic and later England when additional parties emerged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary methods of resolving executive-legislative conflict (resignation or dissolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the executive ministry displeases the House, the House passes an adverse vote; the ministry may resign or dissolve Parliament. If they resign, a new ministry is appointed from the party shown strongest; if they dissolve, a new Parliament is chosen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical virtues and dangers: this method is swift and effective at cutting knots but its swiftness and effectiveness are both a merit and a danger. Upper house conflicts may be remedied by dissolution or, as an extreme, creation of new peers.

rubrics_metrics.name: American methods of resolving conflict: veto, override, and resort to the people
rubrics_metrics.description: If over an executive act the Senate can check the President; if over a bill the President may veto and the two Houses can, by two-thirds majority, pass it over his veto; otherwise the bill drops and the matter is remitted to the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical effect: slower than parliamentary remedies; may fail in crises needing immediate action; ultimate remedy is elections which can establish accord between House and President, but the Senate may remain opposed for longer due to different election timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value placed on executive independence in America despite efficiency loss
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrine that the executive should be wholly independent of the legislative branch — Americans understand this involves loss of power and efficiency but believe it makes greatly for safety in a popular government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expectation: executive and legislature should cooperate as public opinion allows; reliance increasingly placed on executive veto as a protection against hasty legislative decisions; some argue for borrowing elements from parliamentary practice but fear loss of congressional independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning against ministers appearing in the legislature (risk to congressional independence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals that the President's ministers might be permitted to appear in both Houses to answer questions (perhaps to join debate) might lead to ministers being chosen in accord with the party holding a majority in the legislature, undermining congressional independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical example: Norwegian pre-separation experience; cautionary note that small changes can reconstruct larger parts of the constitutional system and erode separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited presidential initiative and influence over Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: The President and his ministers have no initiative in Congress, little influence over Congress, except what they can exert upon individual members through patronage or upon their party in Congress by threatening it with popular displeasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as one of the five practical results of separation; explains why executives often cannot frame or push legislation directly in the U.S. system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional imperfect control over administrative departments
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress has, together with unlimited powers of inquiry, imperfect powers of control over the administrative departments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a consequence: investigative powers exist but control mechanisms are limited, creating gaps in oversight and management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diffusion of responsibility and difficulty of fixing blame
rubrics_metrics.description: The nation does not always know how or where to fix responsibility for misfeasance or neglect; persons and bodies making and executing laws can shift the burden of blame on others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: accountability is blurred under separated systems, weakening direct political responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss of force by friction between branches
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a loss of force by friction — part of the energy, force, and time of the men and bodies that make up the government is dissipated in struggles with one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This friction is inherent to free governments relying on checks; more checks mean more friction and less efficient action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of insufficient executive vigour and promptitude in crises
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a risk that executive vigour and promptitude may be found wanting at critical moments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: in emergencies the separated system may be slow to act; historical example: need for near-dictatorial powers during the U.S. Civil War (Lincoln) to meet exigencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: General lack of unity in a separated government
rubrics_metrics.description: In the American government considered as a whole there is a want of unity: its branches are unconnected; their efforts are not directed to one aim and do not produce one harmonious result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: sailors, helmsman, and engineer do not obey one will; illustrated by historical narrative of the slaveholder struggle culminating in the War of Secession where constitutional machinery failed to solve the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive needs in crises (money and extraordinary powers); parliamentary advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: When a sudden crisis comes the executive needs a large command of money and powers in excess of those allowed at ordinary times; under the European system the Chamber is at once appealed to for supplies and legislation, enabling ministry to act with the weight of the people behind it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In America the President has little routine connection with Congress, which is unaccustomed to executive questions; Congress's machinery and lack of ministerial leaders unfit it for prompt practical response; wartime example: powers used by Lincoln.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core presidential reserved functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain functions remain strictly reserved to the President such as pardoning, making promotions in the army and navy, and negotiating (but not concluding) treaties with foreign states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are among the few areas where the President retains substantial independent authority even when Congress is dominant; treaty conclusion still requires Senate assent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of party majorities on presidential power
rubrics_metrics.description: When one party possesses a large majority in Congress it can overpower the President, taking from him all but a few strictly reserved functions; when parties are evenly divided the President has more freedom though constrained by existing legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical result: 'party in power' in America may have little effective power beyond spoils; party control produces varying degrees of executive effectiveness depending on majorities in the two houses.
